newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire prime minister orders attack on rebels.
newsitem.headline: Zaire prime minister orders attack on rebels.

text.p: Zaire's prime minister told the nation on Monday he had formally ordered the armed forces to launch a counter-offensive to recapture territory held by Tutsi-led rebels in the east.

"In the name of the government and in agreement with the president of the republic, I have today ordered our armed forces to conduct the war and recover regions currently under occupation and restore the authority of the state," Kengo wa Dondo said on state television.

Kengo, whose comments were broadcast before the main evening news, urged the Zairean people to support the armed forces and asked that television and radio programmes reflect this national commitment.
"The sacred duty of every Zairean man and woman is to defend and maintain the nation's territorial integrity," he said.
It was not immediately clear what impact Kengo's comments would have on the timing of the counter-thrust, which has been promised for over a month.
Zairean troops and mercenaries -- said by one dignitary in the region to number 300 -- have been gathering in the eastern town of Kisangani in preparation for the push.
Three Russian-built attack helicopters, bristling with missiles and 24 mm cannon, circled over the town and outlying villages on Sunday and Monday.

Army chief of staff General Mahele Leiko Bokungo, appointed in December with wide-ranging powers, arrived in Kisangani last week. Witnesses report regular arrivals of planes in recent days and weeks with weapons and men.
"It won't be long before this adventure is over," the governor of Upper Zaire, Lombeya Bosongo, told Reuters correspondent William Wallis there on Monday. The governor would not elaborate.
The rebels, who launched their offensive last October, hold towns and territory along the borders with Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda after routing the Zairean army in the east.

Veteran President Mobutu Sese Seko returned home in December after cancer surgery and four months rest in Europe and reshuffled the government and army leadership to bolster the central authorities' response to the rebels.
Apart from his comments on the war, Kengo also pledged to press ahead with Zaire's democratic reforms.
"No person and no event will distance us from our aim of pursuing the democratisation process and organising elections to install the institutions of the third republic," he said.
Under Zaire's much-delayed democratic transition, elections must be held by July. Mobutu, 66, who has returned to Europe for fresh medical tests, plans to stand.

Rebel leader Laurent Kabila is a long-standing foe of Mobutu, who seized power in 1965 and ruled Zaire virtually unchallenged until foreign and domestic pressure forced him to accept democratic reform in 1990.
